what.text: Thymosin alpha-1 (international name thymalfasin) is a chain of 28 amino acids. The drug version is synthetic and has the same structure as the natural peptide first isolated from thymus tissue (“thymosin fraction 5”). It acts on immune cells, especially lymphocytes, and is classed as an immunostimulant.

what.text: Injected under the skin, it reaches its highest blood level in about 6 hours and returns to baseline within 24 hours.

src.label: Zadaxin summary of product characteristics (Italian), AIFA

what.text: Thymosin alpha-1 is an approved medicine in Italy (Zadaxin), but not in the US. It is an immune drug, not a muscle or tissue-repair drug.

research.text: Thymosin alpha-1 has been tested in many human trials, including large ones. A US Phase 3 trial in hepatitis B did not confirm a benefit, and the largest sepsis trial (1,106 people) found no effect on death rates. No trial has tested it for muscle or injury recovery.
Each study is listed below as it was run.

research.title: TESTS: adults with sepsis, 22 centers

facts.v: multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled (NCT02867267)
1,106 adults aged 18 to 85 with sepsis (552 thymosin alpha-1, 554 placebo); 1,089 analyzed
injections under the skin every 12 hours for up to 7 days
main goal: death from any cause within 28 days

research.found: 28-day death rates were 23.4% with thymosin alpha-1 and 24.1% with placebo, no meaningful difference. No secondary or safety outcome differed. Subgroups by age and diabetes hinted at different effects; the authors concluded there was no clear evidence of benefit. The trial was partly funded by SciClone Pharmaceuticals, Zadaxin’s maker, and several authors received grants from it.

src.label: Wu J, et al. BMJ 2025 (TESTS trial)
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02867267

research.title: ETASS: severe sepsis, 6 hospitals

facts.v: multicenter, single-blind, randomized, no placebo (NCT00711620)
361 adults with severe sepsis in intensive care (181 thymosin alpha-1, 180 control)
death from any cause at 28 days; immune markers

research.found: Death rates were 26.0% with thymosin alpha-1 and 35.0% in controls, a borderline result (P = 0.062 in the main analysis). No serious drug-related adverse event was recorded. The larger TESTS trial later found no difference.

src.label: Wu J, et al. Crit Care 2013 (ETASS trial)
Wu J, et al. BMJ 2025 (TESTS trial)

research.title: Chronic hepatitis B, multicenter US trial

facts.v: placebo-controlled, double-blind
97 adults with HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B (49 thymosin alpha-1, 48 placebo)
1.6 mg or placebo twice a week
6 months of treatment, 6 months of follow-up
complete response: virus DNA and HBeAg negative at month 12

research.found: Complete response: 14% on thymosin alpha-1, 4% on placebo (P = 0.084, not significant). The authors wrote that the results “do not confirm” benefits reported in other studies.

src.label: Mutchnick MG, et al. J Viral Hepat 1999

research.title: Chronic hepatitis B, 26 vs 52 weeks of treatment

facts.v: randomized, three groups: 26 weeks, 52 weeks, or no treatment
98 people with chronic hepatitis B
18 months of follow-up
clearance of virus DNA and HBeAg

research.found: At 18 months, complete response was 40.6% with 26 weeks of treatment, 26.5% with 52 weeks and 9.4% untreated. Only the 26-week group differed significantly. No significant side effects were seen.

src.label: Chien RN, et al. Hepatology 1998

research.title: Chronic hepatitis B, 0.8 vs 1.6 mg

facts.v: randomized comparison of two doses; no placebo group
316 people with chronic hepatitis B and raised liver enzymes
24 weeks of treatment, follow-up to 72 weeks
liver enzymes, virus DNA and HBeAg

research.found: Response rates were similar with both doses. All drug reactions were mild; most were changes in liver enzymes.

src.label: Iino S, et al. J Viral Hepat 2005

research.title: COVID-19 prevention in people on dialysis, Kansas City

facts.v: randomized, no placebo; thymalfasin twice a week vs standard care (NCT04428008)
189 people with kidney failure on hemodialysis
8 weeks of treatment, about 4 months of follow-up
COVID-19 infections, hospital stays, deaths

research.found: Posted results: COVID-19 in 5 of 91 treated people and 7 of 98 controls; deaths 3 and 7; serious adverse events 28 and 26. No significance tests were reported in the record.

us.text: Thymosin alpha-1 is not FDA approved for any use. FDA lists it among compounding nominations withdrawn from its safety-risk category, and it is not one of the six peptides in the October 2026 HHS compounding policy. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: none. Drugs@FDA lists no approved drug containing thymalfasin. Zadaxin is approved in Italy, not in the US.

items.text: FDA lists “Thymosin-alpha 1 (Ta1)” among bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn. FDA says compounded thymosin alpha-1 “may pose significant risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration and may have complexities with regard to peptide-related impurities and API characterization. The safety-related information is inadequate for the agency to sufficiently understand the extent of any safety issues raised by the proposed compounded drug.”

world.lead: Thymosin alpha-1 is an approved prescription medicine in Italy (Zadaxin, authorised 1996), where its approved use is as an add-on to flu vaccination in people with weak immune systems. It is not approved in the US, Canada or by the EU centrally.

after.text: Thymosin alpha-1 is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. The list’s S2.3 entry names thymosin-β4 (beta-4) and its derivatives, a different peptide. Class S0 applies only to substances with no current approval by any government health authority; thymosin alpha-1 is approved in Italy. Whether WADA classes it elsewhere was not confirmed. The 2027 list does not name it either.

side.text: In trials and in the Italian label, thymosin alpha-1 has caused few reported side effects, mostly mild injection-site pain. It is an immune drug, so the label urges caution with other immune-modifying medicines.

items.text: no clinically relevant side effects were seen, except occasional mild, short-lived pain at the injection site. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding and in people allergic to it. Caution is advised with other immunomodulating drugs.
